target_description:
Type: Vessel | Class: Shipwreck | Subclass: Wood
Shipwreck City Data
This target has been classified as a wooden boat, resting in 40 feet of water and measuring roughly 55 feet by 14 feet. The dive shows the bow and stern sections largely intact, with structural ribs and framing visible, though the midship area is heavily broken down. A prominent gun mount fitting is visible on the bow, along with hardware including a diamond-shaped fastener and various fittings along the hull. Sponge-like growth colonizes parts of the exposed wood, and a red plastic cup rests among the wreckage, along with visible x-braced framing near the stern.
Prior Research and Theories
This target has been historically explored and logged by Coastal Sensing & Survey under LU12. DCS Films documents it in detail as the Kahlenberg: built in 1913, 50 feet long and 11 feet wide, first used by the U.S. Navy as a tender in Oriental waters, likely during WWI, with the gun mount on the bow a legacy of that service. After being struck from the naval register, it was sold to Kahlenberg Industries Inc., a maker of fishing and towboat engines, who used it as a demonstration boat. Captain Franz Nelson later bought it in Alaska and brought it to Puget Sound to work as a shrimp boat in Elliott Bay, one of several vessels that fished over deep wreck sites there. Its drag net was 15 feet wide and 25 feet long, run off 600 feet of cable by a steam-powered winch, reaching depths of 180 to 300 feet on hauls that covered a quarter mile in about 30 minutes. Nelson ran the boat for years with his wife Elsie and sometimes his son Bill as crew, drawing local press coverage, including one occasion when Ivar Haglund helped bring in a 60-pound octopus pulled up in the net. It was later identified on the bottom of Lake Union by the Maritime Documentation Society and DCS Films, with its midship section destroyed and only the bow and stern remaining, matching what Shipwreck City's own imagery shows.

This target has been classified as a shipwreck, resting in 40 feet of water, with dimensions still to be determined. Shipwreck City has now dived and photographed the site. Dive footage shows a wooden hull with a pointed bow and copper-toned sheathing at the stem, an intact deck with square hatch openings, and a distinctive H-shaped timber bitt, two upright posts joined by a crossbar, matching historical accounts of the vessel's towing gear. 
This target has been historically explored and logged by Coastal Sensing & Survey under LU42. DCS Films documents it by name, recording it at 85 feet long with a 19 foot beam. The Lake Union Virtual Museum also documents the wreck, noting that a diver was able to clear sediment and reveal painted name lettering on the hull, and identifying the timber H-bitt seen in Shipwreck City's photos as the fitting historically used to haul large sailing vessels through Puget Sound.
Additional Context
The J.E. Boyden was built in 1888 and abandoned in 1935, with a depth of hold of 10 feet. She operated during a period when sail and engine power coexisted in Puget Sound, working as a tug to help large sailing ships navigate variable winds and tight waterways, sometimes towing more than one vessel at a time, archival photos even show a group of Makah whalers hitching a ride alongside a larger ship under tow.

Shipwreck City Data
 This target has not yet been explored by the Shipwreck City team, though it has been surveyed and dived by other researchers. The following is compiled from those prior third-party surveys and public records, not our own ROV/dive data.
Target LU62 is logged as the wreck of the Gypsy Queen, per Coastal Sensing & Survey's target log. LU62 is the Wreck of the Gypsy Queen, catalogued alongside neighboring targets in the same survey pass: LU63, a double-ender sailboat, LU64, a wooden pleasure craft, and LU65, a cannery tender. She rests in about 40 feet of water at the south end of Lake Union, sitting upright, as it would have been in her mooring. Original specifications: length of 136 feet, beam 25 feet 7.5 inches, draft 8 feet 6 inches, and it displaced 245 tons. The hull remains coated in algae and mud, but divers have found rooms and corridors, even a mess, still walkable inside the submerged structure.
(Once Shipwreck City conducts its own pass: exact GPS position, current sonar return dimensions, marine growth/biofouling levels, any visible armament mounts or hardware, debris in the surrounding area, and a confirmed current depth — sources conflict between 25 ft and 40 ft.)
Prior Research and Theories
The wreck was first identified and logged in a Coastal Sensing & Survey field entry dated January 28, 2020, covering a five-target cluster (LU62–LU66) in the same area. Earlier still, diver Dan Warter's underwater video, loaded in January 2011, and a companion piece by Chris Borgen documented the wreck in clear conditions, building on the visual record established by the Lake Union Virtual Museum and the DCS Films archive. UW oceanography students later produced a sub-inch-resolution sonar scan of the wreck as part of a seafloor-mapping course. It's not known exactly when the Queen sank in Lake Union, though written accounts place her final owners' plans, and the boat's disappearance, in the years just after 1968.
Additional Context
The YMS-105 was laid down May 13, 1941 by Frank L. Sample Jr. Inc. at Boothbay Harbor, Maine, launched March 10, 1942, and completed that July. She carried one 3-inch .50 caliber anti-aircraft gun, four .50 caliber machine guns, two 20mm guns, and two depth charge projectors, stocking eight 300-pound depth charges, and could reach 15 knots on twin 880-BHP diesel engines. From 1942–1944 she served with the Eastern Sea Frontier, a coastal command patrolling from Canada to Jacksonville under Vice-Admiral Adolphus Andrews, before later duty in the Pacific. She was decommissioned April 17, 1946, and passed through roughly 13 owners — briefly known as the Emerson — before Thomas Stanley "Stan" Hill and his wife Alice bought her in 1958 and renamed her Gypsy Queen. Hill's plan was ambitious: use the Queen as a floating fish-processing plant, pair it with a trawler he named the Gypsy Trader, and tow the whole operation to Alaska with a tug called the Gypsy Too. The plan unraveled in stages — the Gypsy Too burned in 1965, and the Gypsy Trader sank in April 1968 — before the Gypsy Queen herself eventually went down in Lake Union, still fitted with the refrigeration equipment and generators Hill had installed for that final voyage.

Shipwreck City Data
This target has been explored by Shipwreck City but remains unidentified. It is currently classified under debris, with a likely subtype of plane wreck given its metal construction. Resting in 40 feet of water, the object measures roughly 12 feet in length and has a tapered, cylindrical shape consistent with an aircraft wing drop tank. The object is partially submerged in the lakebed sediment, with only its upper surface exposed. A significant breach or damaged section is visible along the midsection, torn open and coated in algae and biofouling around the exposed edges, while the tapered end shows visible flanges and what appear to be plumbing attachments. The extent of the damage makes it difficult to determine whether it occurred on impact, during sinking, or through decades of degradation. A follow-up dive is recommended to confirm the identification and inspect the attachment points and damaged section more closely.
Prior Research and Theories
This target has been logged twice by Coastal Sensing & Survey under LU73: an initial entry from January 28, 2020 recorded simply as an unknown target, and a later entry from August 22, 2021 identifying it as a kayak. That identification differs from the drop-tank theory suggested by the more recent Shipwreck City imagery, so the two accounts should be reconciled on a future dive.
Additional Context
This target has not been historically identified. If confirmed as a drop tank, it would fit a well-documented pattern of these tanks getting a second life after military service. Jettisoned drop tanks from downed or returning aircraft have been repurposed by civilians as boats in multiple documented cases — from Vietnamese farmers who split Vietnam War-era tanks into functional river canoes, still in use decades later, to WWII airmen in the Pacific who built drop-tank multihull sailing racers of their own. If this object saw similar reuse, it may represent a small custom-built or repurposed craft rather than a straightforward discarded tank, which would also help explain the "possible small boat" classification in its original naming.
